Final review of Fono furniture and fixtures held just ahead of Friday’s official opening of offices

2026-10-06

By

Asi Andrew Fa'asau

andrew@samoanews.com

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — Two representatives from Hawaii-based furniture and workplace solutions company SystemCenter recently visited American Samoa to conduct a comprehensive project close-out review and inspect furniture, fixtures, and workplace materials supplied for the new Fono building in Fagatogo. The visit comes ahead of next Friday's official opening of lawmakers' offices, marking a significant milestone in the completion of the multi-million dollar legislative complex and the conclusion of the Fourth Session of the 39th Legislature before lawmakers return in January 2027.

The visiting officials, Tess Camanse-DeCorte, SystemCenter's Vice President of Administration, and Anna Marie Agarpao, the company's Asia/Pacific Rim Project Manager, spent several days meeting with Fono leaders and staff while touring the new Fono building.

Both visitors expressed admiration for the distinctive craftsmanship and architectural vision behind the new Legislature headquarters, designed by renowned architect Mark Lively. Blending modern, state-of-the-art features with the iconic form of the traditional Samoan fale, the building stands as one of the most recognizable landmarks in the Territory. Situated in the heart of downtown Fagatogo, the impressive structure has become the centerpiece of American Samoa's seat of government, bringing together the offices of the Territory's three branches of government within walking distance of one another.

Directly across the main street from the Fono building is the Office of the Governor, which is temporarily operating from the former ANZ Bank building overlooking Fagatogo's historic village green, Malaeoletalu. Nearby stands the new High Court building, home to the Office of the Chief Justice.

“It is always rewarding to see a project completed and being used for the purpose it was intended,” the visitors remarked during discussions with legislative staff. “We understand from Legislature personnel that lawmakers have been without permanent office accommodations since the old Fono building was demolished in 2017. Knowing that our company has played a part in helping provide senators and their constituents with a modern, comfortable, and functional office environment is especially gratifying. It is satisfying to see a space that will support both the work of the Legislature and the people they serve.”

In addition to their salaries, senators and representatives receive a $65,000 annual office expense allowance, while the Senate President and House Speaker receive $85,000 per year. The allowance is intended to cover expenses incurred in the discharge of official legislative duties. Under American Samoa law, legislators are not required to provide an accounting of how the allowance is spent, and it is only taxed if okayed by the lawmaker..

The SystemCenter officials described the new Fono building as an outstanding facility and said the furniture and workplace solutions supplied by SystemCenter complemented the building's interior design seamlessly. According to the visitors, the furnishings integrated naturally with the building's architectural character while enhancing both efficiency and appearance.

The visitors were particularly impressed with the 32 massive posts located inside the legislative chambers, 16 in the Senate chamber and 16 in the House chamber. Each post is adorned with intricate Samoan carvings and traditional motifs that reflect the richness of Samoa's cultural heritage. Together with the siapo-inspired décor featured throughout the chambers, the carvings create an atmosphere that is distinctly Samoan while maintaining the professional setting of a modern legislative institution.

The carvings are the work of one of American Samoa's most respected artists, master carver, and traditional tattoo practitioner, Su'a Uilisone Fitiao. Widely recognized for his contributions to Samoan art and culture, Fitiao's craftsmanship is evident throughout the chambers, where traditional designs have been incorporated into the building's architectural identity. Another traditional feature of construction is the highly prized native Samoan wood, Ifilele, which covers the podiums in both chambers.

Complementing the carvings are the striking siapo designs that adorn the upper walls of the chambers. These were hand-painted on traditional Samoan barkcloth by Fitiao's wife, Regina "Reggie" Meredith-Fitiao, a highly regarded cultural artist, educator, and practitioner of siapo. Reggie is recognized throughout the Pacific for her expertise in traditional barkcloth art and serves as an art professor at the American Samoa Community College. Through her work, she has helped preserve and promote one of Samoa's most treasured cultural art forms while sharing its significance with audiences both locally and abroad.

The visitors also expressed their appreciation to Senate Chief of Staff Faalua Fruean-Tua and members of the Senate staff for their hospitality and assistance throughout their stay. They thanked staff members for taking the time to provide a detailed tour of the facility and for sharing the history, planning, and vision behind the Legislature's new home.

As first-time visitors to American Samoa, both officials said they were grateful for the opportunity to experience the Territory firsthand and gain a deeper understanding of its people, culture, and traditions. They noted that while they had previously worked on projects involving American Samoa from afar, visiting the islands in person provided a far greater appreciation for the unique blend of Samoan culture and modern governance that defines the Territory.

Although this marked their first visit to American Samoa, SystemCenter itself is no stranger to the Territory. The Honolulu-based furniture and workplace solutions company has a longstanding relationship with several local government agencies and institutions.

Among its previous projects, SystemCenter furnished and installed demountable wall systems for the American Samoa Power Authority's headquarters project in 2018. The company has also supplied filing and storage systems for the former High Court building in Fagatogo as well as LBJ Tropical Medical Center.

Founded 50 years ago, Systemcenter is a family-owned, second-generation contract office furniture dealership proudly rooted in Hawaii since 1976. SystemCenter specializes in commercial furniture, workplace planning, interior solutions, project management, delivery, and installation for government, healthcare, education, and corporate clients throughout Hawaii and the Pacific region.

"Our decades of experience reflect a legacy of trust, stability, and a profound understanding of how well-designed work environments can positively impact productivity, collaboration, and overall employee well-being," the company stated on their website.

The company's involvement with the new Fono building began after architect Mark Lively, recommended SystemCenter to Fono leaders as a potential supplier of furniture and related materials.

In June 2024, representatives of the American Samoa Legislature traveled to Honolulu to meet with SystemCenter management and review the company's products and capabilities. Representing the Fono during those discussions were James McGuire, Special Assistant to the President of the Senate, and former House Representative Sam Meleisea.

Following those meetings, the Senate elected to proceed with a contract awarding SystemCenter responsibility for furnishing the Senate chamber and senators' offices in the new building. SystemCenter also supplied various materials incorporated into the building's construction.

McGuire, who was assigned by Senate President Tuaolo Manaia Fruean to monitor construction progress and ensure that work complied with project specifications and design requirements, said the furnishings contributed significantly to the character of the new facility.

"I believe buildings are art," McGuire declared. "I believe the ability of what your company does really adds to the authenticity and the aesthetics of the Fono building. I'm really happy with the lobbies on both the first and second floors."

While neither SystemCenter nor legislative officials provided a detailed inventory of all furnishings installed in the Senate chambers and offices, the company worked closely with project representatives to ensure that furniture selections complemented the building's design and met the operational needs of lawmakers and staff.

As discussions turned to the future, McGuire emphasized that preserving the quality of the multimillion-dollar facility will depend heavily on ongoing upkeep.

"Like all buildings, maintenance is the key to longevity," he said.

The visiting SystemCenter officials agreed, noting that proper care and routine maintenance are essential to maximizing the lifespan of furniture and interior systems.

They said the company remains committed to supporting its clients after installation and will provide maintenance guides and recommendations to help ensure the furniture remains in excellent condition for years to come.

The visitors also agreed with McGuire's observation that the stairway leading to the building's main entrance should be tiled. He said the unfinished concrete steps appear plain and detract from the overall grandeur of the facility.

"This is the architectural crown jewel of Tutuila Island, a project that cost more than $20 million," McGuire said. "It is one of the most significant government investments ever undertaken in American Samoa. A building of this stature deserves tiled steps and walkways leading to its grand entrance."

McGuire also suggested that the area could become a popular location for wedding photography, similar to Samoa's Parliament House at Mulinuu, where newlywed couples often gather for commemorative photos.

He described the new Fono building as a historic achievement that will serve future generations of leaders and residents. While the project took years to complete, he said the end result is something the entire Territory can take pride in.

“Good things are worth waiting for,” McGuire said. “Lawmakers have gone more than ten years without permanent offices, so Friday’s opening marks an important milestone. I hope the new offices will make senators more accessible to their constituents, and I’m confident that both lawmakers and the public will enjoy the comfortable, functional workspace made possible by SystemCenter’s furnishings.”

After completing their inspection and meetings, Tess Camanse-DeCorte and Anna Marie Agarpao returned to Honolulu last Thursday, expressing confidence that the new Fono building will serve the people of American Samoa well for many years to come.

BACKGROUND

Paramount Builders’ original winning bid to build the new Fono was a little over $10 Million.

A final dollar amount for the new Fono facility —Fono building, new office building, fixtures & furniture, and parking lot — has not been revealed yet.

However, an estimate has it at around $38 Million, but this was just for the buildings alone. There are also accounts of unpaid invoices.

Advancing bottomfish research through community partnerships in American Samoa

2026-10-05

Source: NOAA Fisheries

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — NOAA Fisheries, American Samoa’s Department of Marine and Wildlife Resources, and local fishermen recently completed a groundbreaking bottomfish survey in American Samoa! As the management of these important species evolves, we are building strong partnerships with local communities to build up our understanding of bottomfish life history.

The waters of American Samoa are home to a diverse array of marine wildlife, but few species are as commercially and culturally significant as the region’s bottomfish complex. Bottomfish are deep-water species that live at or near the ocean floor. They’re one of the primary sources of protein for residents of American Samoa, where grocery stores can be few and far between.

Historically, scientists have assessed American Samoa’s bottomfish species together as a multi-species complex to determine population health and fishing limits. Following an independent peer review in 2023, the assessment shifted toward assessing the following six key species individually:

    •    Etelis coruscans (Palu-loa, also known as onaga or longtail red snapper)

    •    Etelis carbunculus (Palu-malau, also known as ehu or ruby snapper)

    •    Etelis boweni (Palu-malau, also known as giant ehu or giant ruby snapper, and often not differentiated from Etelis carbunculus)

    •    Aphareus rutilans (Palu-gutusiliva, also known as lehi or silverjaw snapper)

    •    Pristipomoides flavipinnis (Palu-sina, also known as goldeneye snapper)

    •    Pristipomoides zonatus (Palu-ula, also known as gindai or oblique-banded snapper)

The 2023 independent review also highlighted the need for more species-specific biological information to support future assessments of key species in the bottomfish complex.

Developing species-specific assessments requires information on reproduction, age, growth, and other life-history components. Collecting these data improves our scientific understanding of these important fish and provides better information to support sustainable fisheries management.

A SHARED PURPOSE

As the NOAA Fisheries team began planning for its first survey, they made sure to engage early and often with American Samoa’s Department of Marine and Wildlife Resources and local communities.

In February 2026, scientists from the Pacific Islands Fisheries Science Center traveled to American Samoa and organized fisher participation from Tutuila and the Manuʻa Islands. They met with local communities, talked about the bottomfish fishery and the survey, and showed them the sampling gear and how it would be used. American Samoa residents also played an active role in designing the survey.

“The most successful way to manage these stocks is to engage the local fishermen,” says Dr. Eva Schemmel, a fisheries biologist with the Pacific Islands Fisheries Science Center. “They’re the ones managing this resource on a daily basis. Collaborating with them not only helps them understand the science that goes into management, it also makes the science better because of the local insight and perspectives they bring.”

Before the start of the survey, the NOAA Fisheries team returned to the islands to reconvene with community members and conduct some shore-based sampling of bottomfish from local fishers. The scientists joined American Samoan fishermen in small boats to collect biological samples and worked alongside Department of Marine and Wildlife Resources staff at the third Pago Pago Open Fishing Tournament. Bottomfish were a category for the first time in the tournament, and scientists were able to directly biosample fish there.

The NOAA Fisheries team also trained local fishery representatives to remove fish otoliths (structures of the inner ear that allow us to estimate fish age) and gonads (reproductive organs). This ensured that biosampling will continue even after the conclusion of the survey. In just that 1 week, the teams collected samples from 120 fish.

A NEW ERA OF BOTTOMFISH MONITORING

After months of planning and coordination with American Samoa’s Department of Marine and Wildlife Resources, the survey officially kicked off with the arrival of the NOAA ship Oscar Elton Sette. The NOAA Fisheries scientists were joined by Manu’a Islands fishers Clint Ilaoa and Keith AhSoon and Department of Marine and Wildlife Resources representative Shaun Laolagi. The collaborative team spent 15 days at sea and collected more than 900 biological samples. They met their sampling goals and generated a comprehensive dataset that will strengthen future research and stock assessments in this region.

Scientists also conducted genetic sampling for 100 of the Palu-loa (Etelis coruscans) collected during the survey. These sampling efforts aim to develop alternative, epigenetic ageing methods where age can be estimated from small tissue samples. If successful, this new method for estimating the age of Palu-loa will reduce future sampling costs and allow us to update life history assessments more efficiently.

NOAA Fisheries scientist Kristen Dahl (right) holds a Palu-loa, or onaga (Etelis coruscans), alongside local fisher Keith AhSoon. [Photo: Jamie Barlow/NOAA Fisheries]

The information we collected during this survey is invaluable and contributes to our understanding of these important species. The American Samoa bottomfish fishery has a diverse species assemblage. The team observed that fish species were consistently caught and distributed by depth. There was a clear delineation in habitat ranges, potentially due to competition or ecological niches keeping species separate.

American Samoa’s bottomfish fishery was last surveyed 10 years ago, and that survey was the primary source of bottomfish biological samples to date. Combined, the samples collected during this year's survey are sufficient to start drafting life history profiles for all six bottomfish management unit species, filling critical scientific gaps. The NOAA Fisheries team is now processing all of the samples in Honolulu.

COMMUNITY-CENTERED SCIENCE

The partnerships NOAA Fisheries scientists developed and strengthened through this survey effort were just as significant as the data collected. “The way fisheries are assessed in American Samoa and across the Pacific Islands is changing, and those changes are centered on local fisheries,” Schemmel says.

One of the aspects of this survey that Schemmel found particularly impactful was the successful distribution of sampled fish back into communities on five of the islands of American Samoa. NOAA Fisheries visited each of these islands at the survey’s conclusion with the Department of Marine and Wildlife Resources, who delivered sampled fish to each island’s matai (family chief). The matai, in turn, allocated fish to members of the community.

This exchange ensured fish from the survey were not wasted, and also provided NOAA Fisheries scientists with a valuable opportunity to engage directly with the community. “The matai and the whole community would come out to greet us when we brought these fish with the Department of Marine and Wildlife Resources,” Schemmel says. “It gave us the chance to talk to them about what we’re doing and why.”

“Seeing the science behind our fish stocks, while also being able to give the catch back to our communities, encourages us to continue caring for both the land and sea,” adds Keith AhSoon, a fisher from Manuʻa who was involved with the survey.

“On behalf of the Department of Marine and Wildlife Resources, faʻafetai tele [thank you very much] to the whole NOAA Fisheries team,” says Nathan Ilaoa, director of the Department of Marine and Wildlife Resources. “They worked hard out there in rough conditions, and they did it the right way, with local fishermen and our Department staff alongside them, with the fish caught going to our communities of Tutuila and Manuʻa. We are so grateful for the partnership with the Pacific Islands Fisheries Science Center and we're ready to keep building on it.”

Fisheries monitoring is not just one survey. It’s a collaborative effort that lasts years to better understand the fishery from all sectors—recreational to commercial—and across the entire region. Schemmel hopes that this is just the beginning for cultivating cooperative efforts in American Samoa. “This survey not only collected critical life history information we need, it jump-started fisheries monitoring in this region, and it did it in a community-forward way,” she says.

American Samoa student to represent territory at 2026 National Civics Bee in Washington D.C.

2026-10-01

(Source: CoC- American Samoa)

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — The American Samoa Chamber of Commerce  announces that Shalidiloya Faavaoga of South Pacific Academy will represent American Samoa at the 2026 National Civics Bee® Championship on Wednesday, October 14, 2026, in Washington, D.C.

Shalidiloya earned second place in American Samoa's local National Civics Bee competition, hosted by the American Samoa Chamber of Commerce in partnership with the U.S. Chamber of Commerce Foundation.

The local competition was held on July 25, 2026, at South Pacific Academy, bringing together 30 young participants in a competition designed to strengthen civic knowledge, critical thinking, communication and community engagement.

Klein Garcia of South Pacific Academy earned first place, followed by Shalidiloya Faavaoga in second place and Morena Gurr in third place.

Due to travel arrangements, Klein is unable to make the trip to Washington, D.C. Shalidiloya will therefore travel to the nation’s capital to represent American Samoa at the National Championship.

For the Chamber, the opportunity represents something much larger than a competition. It gives a young person from American Samoa an opportunity to carry the Territory's name, culture and perspective onto a national platform.

AMERICAN SAMOA JOINS STUDENTS FROM ACROSS THE NATION

The 2026 National Civics Bee Championship will bring together 52 middle school finalists representing all 50 states, Washington, D.C., and American Samoa.

The U.S. Chamber of Commerce Foundation reports that more than 20,000 students from 240 communities participated in this year’s competition. Students advanced through competitions organized in partnership with chambers of commerce and other organizations across the country.

For the Chamber, the opportunity represents something much larger than a competition. It gives a young person from American Samoa an opportunity to carry the Territory's name, culture and perspective onto a national platform.

CHAMBER THANKS U.S. CHAMBER FOUNDATION FOR PARTNERSHIP

The American Samoa Chamber of Commerce extends its sincere appreciation to the U.S. Chamber of Commerce Foundation for its partnership and for including American Samoa in this nationwide civic education initiative.

The expansion of the National Civics Bee to all 50 states, Washington, D.C., and American Samoa comes as the United States marks its 250th anniversary in 2026, creating an opportunity for young people from communities throughout the country and Territory to participate in civic education and engagement.

For American Samoa, that inclusion means a local student will stand alongside students from throughout the United States while bringing a uniquely Samoan perspective to the national conversation.

“We are grateful to the U.S. Chamber of Commerce Foundation for giving our students this opportunity,” Gurr said. “Partnerships like this allow our children to see that where they come from does not limit where they can go.”

THANKING OUR PARENTS, SCHOOL AND BUSINESS COMMUNITY

The Chamber also recognizes that opportunities such as this are possible only through strong community support.

The Chamber extends its appreciation to the parents and families of the students who encouraged them, helped them prepare and supported their participation throughout the competition.

Special recognition is also extended to South Pacific Academy, its leadership and teachers. All three of American Samoa’s top local finishers — Klein Garcia, Shalidiloya Faavaoga and Morena Gurr — are students of South Pacific Academy.

The Chamber further thanks its members, sponsors and the American Samoa business community for supporting the local Civics Bee and investing in opportunities for the Territory’s young people.

“When our businesses invest in education and civic leadership, they are investing in the future workforce, entrepreneurs, professionals and leaders of American Samoa,” Gurr said. “These students will one day inherit the responsibility of moving our Territory forward.”

SPECIAL SEND-OFF AND BLESSING

Prior to Shalidiloya’s departure, the American Samoa Chamber of Commerce held a special send-off recognizing her achievement and the responsibility she will carry as American Samoa’s representative.

The Chamber was honored to have Lieutenant Governor Pulumata‘ala Ae Ae Jr. present on behalf of the American Samoa Government and Governor Pulaali‘i Nikolao Pula. The Chamber expressed its appreciation for his support and encouragement of American Samoa’s young people.

As part of the send-off, the Chamber shared Joshua 1:9 as a scripture of encouragement:

“Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the Lord thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest.”

The message reflects the Chamber’s hope that Shalidiloya will travel with courage, confidence and faith as she represents her family, school and Territory.

CARRYING AMERICAN SAMOA TO WASHINGTON

As Shalidiloya prepares to travel to Washington, D.C., the Chamber is encouraging the entire Territory to support her.

“This young lady will be walking onto that national stage carrying more than her own name,” Gurr said. “She carries her family, her school, her village and American Samoa with her.”

“Our message to Shalidiloya is simple: Go with courage. Go with confidence. Go with faith. Carry our flag proudly and show them what the young people of American Samoa can do.

2026 AMERICAN SAMOA NATIONAL CIVICS BEE WINNERS

First Place: Klein Garcia — South Pacific Academy

Second Place: Shalidiloya Faavaoga — South Pacific Academy

Third Place: Morena Gurr — South Pacific Academy

The American Samoa Chamber of Commerce congratulates all of the students who participated in this year’s local competition and wishes Shalidiloya Faavaoga safe travels and success as she represents American Samoa at the 2026 National Civics Bee Championship in Washington, D.C., on October 14.

Acting Chair of ASTCA Board of Directors has stepped down

2026-09-30

By

Asi Andrew Fa'asau

andrew@samoanews.com

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — The Acting Chairman of the American Samoa Telecommunications Authority (ASTCA) Board of Directors, Saena Omar Shalhout, has stepped down from his position to concentrate on his campaign for a seat in the House of Representatives.

In a resignation letter submitted to Governor Pulaali’i Nikolao Pula on September 25, Shalhout announced that his decision was effective immediately.

According to the letter, the decision came after careful reflection and prayer as he weighed his responsibilities as both Acting Chairman and member of the ASTCA Board.

“After careful consideration and praying for the appropriate decision on my status as the Acting Chair of the ASTCA Board and as a Board member, I have decided to resign effective immediately,” Shalout wrote.

Shalhout outlined his years of service to the telecommunications authority, noting that he served on the ASTCA Board from 2018 through 2023. He was later reappointed to the Board on July 31, 2025, and again on September 10, 2026.

He expressed gratitude to Governor Pulaali’i for the confidence placed in him, both as a board member and as Acting Chairman. He also thanked the governor for reappointing the board and allowing its members to continue serving the territory.

While explaining the reasons behind his resignation, Shalhout pointed to the demands of the ongoing midterm election campaign for the Maoputasi No. 4 House seat, which includes the villages of Leloaloa, Atu’u, and Satala.

He noted that the board selected on September 10, 2026, has not yet held its first meeting and expressed hope that another member would step forward to assume the chairmanship.

“With this year’s midterm election, I am one of the official candidates and would like to prioritize my daily focus on outreach efforts and engagement with residents in the district,” he stated.

Shalhout said he remains confident that ASTCA will continue moving forward under new leadership. He praised the board’s work and said the authority is well-positioned to build upon its existing achievements while advancing projects aimed at strengthening telecommunications services and supporting economic diversification in American Samoa.

He concluded his letter by thanking the governor for what he described as the privilege of serving the territory through ASTCA.

“I look forward to seeing the continued progress and impact of ASTCA in the years to come,” he wrote.

Saena Omar Shalhout is one of four candidates seeking election to represent Maoputasi No. 4 District in the House of Representatives. The race also includes Talali Perry T. Loloaso, Wightman-Uia Tapai Alailepule, and incumbent Representative Ben Vaivao, setting up a competitive contest for the district seat in the upcoming election.

Butler explains in detail entities involved in the $10 Mil investment in the UAE

2026-09-28

Possibility is raised that Butler’s testimony exposes Governor to impeachment

By

Asi Andrew Fa'asau

andrew@samoanews.com

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — The Senate Government Operations Committee last Friday continued its investigation into the American Samoa Government’s $10 million investment in a United Arab Emirates pension fund, focusing on the details of the transaction and the entities involved in facilitating the investment.

Testimony by Brett Butler, Executive Advisor for Finance in the Governor's Office, during the hearing, according to the Chairman of the Senate committee, raised the possibility that Governor Pulaali'i Nikolao Pula could be possibly exposed to impeachment proceedings.

Butler was questioned extensively about the structure of the investment and the government's involvement in the deal, when he was once again called to testify before the Senate GO Committee.

Committee Chairman Sen. Togiola T.A. Tulafono opened the hearing by outlining three key issues that, in the committee's view, required further clarification.

FIRST

Sen. Togoila pointed to a letter from McKinley Beech Tree (MBT) dated September 18, 2026, the same day the first tranche of the investment was scheduled to be disbursed, informing the American Samoa Government that the closing had been delayed. He said the committee was seeking clarification on the relationship between the entity and the company directly involved in negotiating the investment agreement with the UAE government, and whether their respective roles and responsibilities had been clearly defined throughout the transaction process.

SECOND

The Chair noted that the letter, signed by MBT Director Gregory Burkholder, stated that several discrepancies had been identified in the closing settlement statement. However, the correspondence did not specify the nature of those discrepancies or explain how they affected the transaction. He also noted that the letter stated the transaction could not proceed until the identified discrepancies had been resolved.

THIRD

Togiola then raised concerns about the insurance coverage backing the investment, specifically the role of South Pacific Insurance. He said the committee's investigation had determined that the company is owned by ASG's Insurance Commissioner, prompting questions about potential conflicts of interest and the insurer's financial capacity. He asked whether ASG had conducted its own due diligence on the company and whether officials were satisfied that South Pacific Insurance possessed sufficient assets to reimburse the government's $10 million investment should the transaction fail due to unforeseen circumstances.

In response, Brett Butler explained that ASG initially entered into an agreement with McKinley Investments. According to Butler, McKinley subsequently partnered with Beech Tree, a Texas-based company that serves as the front-end entity for the investment initiative currently under discussion with the UAE government.

“That is why you hear the term McKinley Beech Tree, or MBT,” Butler explained. “You have the leadership of these two companies coming together for this transaction with the UAE government.”

Butler further explained that another entity, referred to as a "monetizer," operates between MBT and the UAE government. He said the selected monetizer is the only party with direct lines of communication to UAE government officials regarding the transaction.

Butler said there are approximately six or seven monetizers available, and that MBT determines which monetizer will be used in its dealings with the UAE government.

According to Butler, the selected monetizer is responsible for submitting the required documentation to the UAE government, which then determines when the investment "window of opportunity" opens and when funding will be released.

Responding to Togiola's question about whether ASG's agreement was with McKinley alone or with both McKinley and Beech Tree, Butler said government officials communicate with the leadership of both companies.

However, he emphasized that while Beech Tree participates in the transaction through its partnership with McKinley, the contractual relationship remains between the ASG and McKinley, making McKinley the entity responsible for final decisions regarding the investment.

Senator Togiola also raised questions about another entity created specifically for the transaction, the Special Purpose Corporation (SPC).

In response, Brett Butler explained that once the UAE government approves the investment, the return funds will initially be deposited into an account in Dubai. After those funds are received by McKinley, a separate company will be established, with ASG holding a 51 percent ownership stake. The company would then open an account at a Swiss bank, where the investment return funds would be deposited.

Butler said the ownership structure would allow ASG to monitor the account and verify the amount of money it contains.

"So the expectation is, the $100 million investment return funds will go there, and we will be able to transfer the tranches of $20 million, $30 million, and $50 million from the Swiss account to the ASG account in Zions Bank," Butler testified.

Asked whether the SPC had already been incorporated and legally established under Swiss law, Butler said the process had not yet been completed because the parties were still awaiting signatures. He added that ASG had withheld its signature pending assurances that it would retain a 51 percent ownership interest, thereby ensuring full visibility into the account and its transactions.

Togiola then asked whether McKinley had provided a timeline for the SPC's formal registration. Butler replied that after McKinley identified discrepancies in the closing settlement statement, it notified the monetizer that the issues would have to be resolved before the closing package could be submitted.

According to Butler, those issues have since been corrected, and the revised closing statement was submitted to the UAE government early last week.

"So right now, we're waiting for the UAE to officially tell us when they're going to fund or open the window of funding," Butler said. "That's where we currently stand."

Togiola asked Butler to identify the monetizer responsible for negotiating the investment transaction with the UAE government.

Butler replied that the company's name was difficult to pronounce because it was foreign, but said he could provide documentation to verify the monetizer's identity and legitimacy.

He explained that the monetizer serves as the direct point of contact with the UAE government, while McKinley Beech Tree (MBT) communicates directly with the monetizer and, in turn, reports developments back to the American Samoa

GOVERNMENT

Togiola then asked for an update on when ASG could expect to receive the first tranche of the investment returns, noting that the originally anticipated payment date of September 18, 2026, had passed without any funds being received.

Butler responded that officials were expecting the UAE funding window to open either Monday or Tuesday.

"When they open up that window, we have, I would say, no more than 72 hours to have them send the funds from the UAE to the MBT Dubai account, and from there to the Swiss account," Butler explained.

He added that discussions were also underway to expedite the transfer of the government's initial $10.1 million investment.

"So that's the timing right now," Butler said. "We are also in discussion with them to get the $10.1 million here immediately because of the stress we are facing."

Senate President Tuaolo Manaia Fruean questioned Butler about the cost of the insurance coverage obtained for the investment. Butler responded that ASG paid between $200,000 and $300,000 for the insurance wrap.

Butler also disputed suggestions that the ASG Insurance Commissioner had any connection to South Pacific Insurance or involvement in the transaction. According to Butler, the commissioner was neither associated with the company nor involved in any aspect of the investment arrangement.

He explained that ASG was unwilling to release the $10.1 million investment without first securing an insurance wrap to protect the funds. As a result, MBT sought out an insurance provider and ultimately engaged South Pacific Insurance, a Louisiana-based company that, by coincidence, also maintains an office in American Samoa.

Tuaolo then asked whether ASG had sought legal advice from the Attorney General's Office before proceeding with the transaction.

Butler replied that while the government did not obtain a formal legal opinion from the Attorney General, it did seek legal guidance from an escrow attorney retained to ensure the terms and conditions of the escrow agreement were properly followed.

According to Butler, multiple legal reviews were conducted before the funds were transferred.

"When we sent the money out, we received several legal opinions, not from the Attorney General, but from the escrow lawyer we approached to make sure the terms of the escrow were followed," Butler said.

He emphasized that the government did not release the funds until it had received the insurance policy, which he said was a prerequisite for proceeding with the investment transaction.

Chair Sen. Togiola asked Butler to identify the Kansas-based escrow attorney consulted by the government during the transaction process. Butler identified the attorney as Timothy Stein.

Togiola followed up by asking whether Butler was aware of the legal requirement that contracts entered into by the government must be reviewed and approved by the Chief Procurement Officer.

Butler replied that he had only learned the day before that all government contracts are required to go through the CPO's office.

"But these types of contracts, I mean the authority I took to do that, sir, was under the Governor's authority," Butler said.

Togiola then challenged that assertion, questioning the legal basis for bypassing established procurement procedures.

"What is the legal authority of the Governor to make independent contracts without following our procurement laws?" Togiola asked.

Butler said he could not answer the question and would need to seek legal advice regarding the Governor's authority in such matters.

He maintained, however, that the transaction did not involve the procurement of goods or services and should instead be viewed as an investment participation agreement.

Butler reiterated that his involvement stemmed from his role as the Governor's economic and finance advisor and that his objective was to secure an investment opportunity for the territory.

"We were not procuring anything," Butler told the committee, explaining that he viewed the arrangement as an investment transaction rather than a procurement contract.

He further stated that Governor Pulaali'i had raised the matter with the AG’s Office during the course of the negotiations. However, Butler said he was unaware of whether the Governor had also consulted with the Chief Procurement Officer regarding the transaction.

Sen. Togiola also questioned Butler about a meeting he had referenced in previous testimony concerning the investment arrangement. The meeting involved Butler, AG Gwen Tauiliili-Langkilde, and members of the McKinley management team during a video conference call.

Butler testified that throughout the virtual meeting, members of the McKinley management group never activated their cameras or otherwise revealed their identities on screen.

He said he could not say whether the decision was intentional, but acknowledged that their refusal to appear on camera raised concerns for the Attorney General.

According to Butler, AG Tauiliili-Langkilde's suspicions deepened when representatives of McKinley later contacted her through a personal email account rather than an official business email address.

Butler said the combination of the officials' unwillingness to show their faces during the video conference and their use of a personal email account prompted the AG to question the legitimacy of the individuals involved and the manner in which communications were being conducted.

Togiola then turned his attention to Butler's authority to execute an agreement of such magnitude on behalf of the American Samoa Government.

Butler testified that the authority he relied upon came directly from the Governor.

The senator pressed further, asking whether Butler could identify any statute, executive order, or other legal authority that expressly authorized him to sign the agreement in the name of and on behalf of ASG.

"I've not seen any legal authority that authorizes me to do that specifically, sir," Butler replied. "I just took direction from the governor."

Togiola further asked whether the Governor had explicitly instructed him that he could proceed with signing the agreement on behalf of the government.

Butler responded that after reviewing the insurance wrap, the agreement itself, and the discussions surrounding the proposed investment, the Governor gave him permission to execute the document.

Seeking clarification, Togiola asked whether that authorization had been provided in writing.

Butler answered that it had not.

According to Butler, the authorization was given verbally by the Governor rather than through a written directive, executive order, or other formal delegation of authority.

The hearing took a sharper turn when Senator Togiola raised the potential legal implications of Butler's testimony regarding the Governor's verbal authorization.

"Mr. Butler, do you realize that in saying what you just said to the Senate, that these are very probable grounds for impeachment of the Governor?" Togiola asked

Butler declined to comment on the legal ramifications of the Governor's actions, saying his focus had been on securing what he believed to be a beneficial investment opportunity for the territory.

"At the end of the day, this is a very good deal for American Samoa, and if how he did this was incorrect in the eyes of our leaders, I'm not here to answer that question, sir," Butler replied. "I think this is a question the leaders should discuss with the Governor and take to that point. But the focus is trying to bring something that will help the territory, and that's what we are focused on."

Togiola concluded his line of questioning by clarifying that he was not seeking a legal opinion from Butler, but rather emphasizing the significance of the testimony that had just been given before the Senate.

He noted that Butler's statements had raised the possibility that the Governor could be exposed to impeachment proceedings if it were determined that proper legal authority had not been followed.

"Which makes me wonder if you understood the consequences, or the potential consequences, of your statements," Togiola said.

Legislation to safeguard U.S. fishing passes U.S. House

2026-09-25

Source: Congresswoman Uifa’atali Amata’s D.C. staff

Washington, D.C. — Congresswoman Uifa’atali Amata is welcoming House passage by voice vote of the Senate companion to a bill she cosponsored in the House for better science-based U.S. fishing safeguards. This amended bill includes much of the original House bill, and it has been returned to the Senate for one final vote to become law.

Last week, the House amended and passed S. 283, the Illegal Red Snapper and Tuna Enforcement Act. This bill overlaps and incorporates policies from its companion House bill, the Amata-cosponsored Standards for Understanding Source and Habitat Identification (SUSHI) Act, H.R. 3706, voted earlier through the House Natural Resources (HNR) Committee, as well as its Subcommittee on Water, Wildlife, and Fisheries, where Amata serves. HNR Chairman Bruce Westerman then managed House passage of S. 283 for the floor vote.

Both the final bill, and its companion effort, are bipartisan and work to secure American seafood using the same method against Illegal, Unreported, and Unregulated (IUU) fishing, which unfairly costs and competes with the American tuna industry, along with other seafood.

The bill requires the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) to develop a standard methodology for identifying the country of origin of seafood to support enforcement against IUU fishing to stop seafood fraud and the problem of U.S. imports of competing IUU product.

“This is a good bipartisan effort to safeguard U.S. tuna, and protect American Samoa’s share of the market, by better identifying IUU produced tuna and preventing American imports of illegal competition that undercut our fishing,” said Congresswoman Amata. “As part of our national food security, we need a dependable U.S. fishing supply that’s not forced to compete against fraudulent IUU bad actors. I appreciate key leaders on both sides of the aisle recognizing the need for this initiative to help keep our fishing competitive. We’re at the finish line for this bill, and I expect final passage of this priority.”

The Senate bill was sponsored by Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX) with Sen. Brian Schatz (D-HI), while the House bill was sponsored in February by Rep. Brian Babin (R-TX) with two original cosponsors, Rep. Aumua Amata (American Samoa) and Rep. Eugene Vindman (D-VA). Along with Pacific fishing, the Gulf waters off the coast of Texas also include fishing for a species of red snapper and tuna.

Legislation Highlights:

•    Directs federal agencies to jointly develop a standard methodology, based on chemical analysis, to identify the country of origin of seafood and support enforcement against IUU fishing and seafood fraud.

•    Requires the methodology to meet the needs of federal and state law enforcement, reduce processing time, and use a portable field kit that can be carried by one person.

•    Requires pilot studies using red snapper and tuna to test the methodology across both stationary and highly migratory fish stocks.

•    Directs agencies, to the extent practicable, to further develop a methodology capable of testing prepared seafood, including ceviche, sashimi, sushi, and poke.

ASCC-PTK holds Fall 2026 Induction Ceremony

2026-09-23

By

James Kneubuhl, ASCC Press Officer

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — Since 1979, the American Samoa Community College (ASCC) has hosted the Alpha Epsilon Mu chapter of the national Phi Theta Kappa (PTK) Honor Society. The PTK's nonprofit mission is to recognize and promote student academic achievement. The Honor Society provides opportunities to cultivate professional and leadership skills, secure scholarships, explore diverse career paths, and build a network of supportive peers and trusted advisors that last a lifetime. The ASCC chapter of the PTK held its induction ceremony for fall 2026 on Friday, September 18, with more than 30 students joining the prestigious Honor Society.

Each semester, the ASCC PTK advisors send membership invitations to qualifying students at the College, which are mostly accepted enthusiastically.

The ASCC Chapter Advisors are Mr. Kuki Tuiasosopo, Chairperson of the Fine Arts Department and Lead Faculty Advisor; Dr. Ernestina Seiuli, Chairperson of the Computer Science Department; and Mrs. Amete Mulipola Moefiainu, Chairperson of the Math Department. Mrs. Adrien Vasai-Moana, former Social Science instructor who now Director of the ASG Office of Vocational & Rehabilitation, serves as an Honorary Advisor.

PTK induction ceremonies include a guest speaker, often an Honor Society alumnus, who shares their experience during and after their pursuit of higher education.  This semester, Jennet Chang-Berquist, a former member of PTK and a 2017 ASCC graduate who now works for ASCC Land Grant as a Horticulture Research Assistant, gave the keynote address.

Chang-Berquist cites her greatest achievements as her scientific research publications and her outreach work representing the Land Grant research program. She gave her talk the amusing title “So What?” and used it to promote the idea that individual achievements have great value, but take on an even greater value when they can be shared to benefit not just the individual but also the wider community.

The program continued with the introduction of the inductees, the ceremonial lighting of candles representing the “flame of knowledge”, and the presenting of the PTK stoles and certificates of membership, for which Dr. Emilia Le’i, Dean of Student Services, provided assistance.

Inductees into the Phi Theta Kappa honor society at ASCC display their lit candles, which represent the "flame of knowledge". The Fall 2025 PTK induction ceremony took place last week, Friday, September 18th, at the College. [Photo: J. Kneubuhl]

Welcomed into the PTK this semester were:

El-Hannora Jayrahmahdai Toimoana, Hana Popili Savaiinanea, Glorius Litalina Lisala, Lui Leitu, Jahnala Sally Mamea, Audrey Leute Valaau, Steel Filiotagata Patane, Aigalesala AJ Herman Leiato, Roman Joseph Faumuina, Ruiyi Shi, Silina Fiso, Joann Tema, Princessvalentine Taufaito’a Vaoga, Tinica Fualolinalufi Oliver, Mauer Osa, Florensenior Amituana’i, Alexis Janahval Uluvalu Tuitoelau-Savea, Manufou Tiana Lotulelei, Alvina Savali, Saina Baker Taumaoe, Alshadai Sopo Siaosi, Desiree Matile Selesele, Rynette Tamasailau Urahono, Tiresaleesetaoealofamoni Harmony Tupule, Emirina Ioane, Akosina Talei Limaono, Immaculate Theresa Sagote, Faasalafa Tauveve Schuster, PJ Isaako, Salome Puanani Elisara, and J-la Vaegafa Afia.

Following the inductees’ reciting of the PTK Pledge, ASCC Dean of Academic Affairs Dr. Siaumaua Ropeti took the podium to give her words of encouragement.

This also gave the PTK an opportunity to express their appreciation for the longstanding support of Dr. Ropeti, who has announced her upcoming retirement.

The Dean was presented with the Phi Theta Kappa Stole of Gratitude, an honor reserved exclusively for college administrators who have contributed significantly to the advancement and success of a PTK chapter.

Crafted from blue satin and finished with a gold embroidered seal featuring the Greek letters of the honor society, the stole symbolizes the lasting bond between Dr. Ropeti and the PTK fellowship of scholars.

For more information on the PTK Honor Society, visit their web page at www.ptk.org.

Sixteen Years Ahead of His Time: Eni Faleomavaega’s Vision for American Samoa’s Ocean Future

2026-09-22

By

by Michael J. McDonald,

American Pacific Resources

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — In American Samoa, we remember Congressman Eni Faleomavaega for many things: his decades of public service, his commanding voice in Washington, his advocacy for Pacific peoples, and his insistence that our small islands should never be treated as an afterthought in decisions affecting the Pacific.

But there is another part of Eni’s legacy that deserves renewed attention today.

More than fifteen years ago, Eni was asking a remarkably forward-looking question: What lies beneath the waters surrounding America and its Pacific territories— and shouldn’t we find out?

Today, in 2026, American Samoa is discussing a Proposed Leasing Notice from the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management for a potential offshore critical-minerals lease sale in federal waters near our islands.

The subject may seem new.

For Eni Faleomavaega, it was not.

HE SAW THE STRATEGIC IMPORTANCE EARLY

By 2010 and 2011, Eni was already raising concerns about seabed minerals and America's growing dependence on foreign sources of critical materials.

At a September 2011 congressional hearing examining China's dominance of rare earth minerals, Eni warned that America's dependence on China posed risks to both national security and economic well-being.

But he did more than identify the problem.

He asked whether America had taken the time to understand the resources potentially available within its own jurisdiction — including around the U.S. territories.

During that hearing, Eni specifically discussed the mineral wealth of the Pacific seabed, describing manganese nodules containing cobalt, manganese, copper and other elements distributed throughout the Pacific.

His own words are striking today.

Speaking at the September 2011 hearing, Eni told his colleagues:

“We call it seabed minerals: Manganese nodules that contain cobalt, manganese, copper, so many other different rare elements, quite extensive throughout the Pacific region.”

He then identified what he believed was missing from the national discussion: “We have not done a very good job in putting our focus on this issue.”

His question was fundamentally one of knowledge: Do we actually know what we have?

That question remains extraordinarily relevant sixteen years later.

ENI'S ANSWER WAS EXPLORATION AND SCIENCE

In 2011, Eni introduced H.R. 2803.

The legislation would have directed the Department of the Interior, acting through the federal offshore energy agency that preceded today's BOEM structure, to conduct a technological capability assessment, seabed survey and economic feasibility study regarding non-fuel minerals in America's shallow and deep seabed.

Importantly for us, his proposal specifically contemplated areas associated with the United States territories and possessions.

And this was not a subject Eni discovered in 2011. A year earlier, while chairing a congressional hearing on the South Pacific, he deliberately looked beyond the immediate issue of tuna and toward the long-term significance of the ocean itself.

He said, “I even understand in the Samoan Islands there is cobalt found there.”

Then he explained the broader vision: “So not just fishing, tuna, but on a more long-term vision in terms of looking at these island countries, as small as they may be, beyond just fishing for tuna.”

And he put a direct question to the federal government:

“Does our Government have any interest in this area besides just tuna, the worth of manganese nodules in the seabeds of these island countries throughout the Pacific?”

Think about what that meant.

Eni was not proposing that America simply rush into the Pacific and start mining. He was proposing that America survey, assess, study and understand.

Before making decisions about resources, we should first know what resources exist.

Before debating their economic potential, we should understand their characteristics.

Before deciding what should or should not happen in the future, we should develop the scientific information necessary to make an informed decision.

That distinction matters enormously today.

FROM 2011 TO 2026

Sixteen years later, the federal government is finally asking many of the questions Eni was raising.

BOEM's current process for American Samoa concerns a potential critical-minerals lease sale on the federal Outer Continental Shelf.

The Proposed Leasing Notice released in July is another step in that process. But a lease sale is not authorization to begin commercial mining.

BOEM itself explains that the environmental review conducted at this stage covers leasing and certain preliminary activities — surveys and activities intended to characterize the environment without significant adverse impacts to natural resources.

Any future testing, delineation or mining would require additional plans, federal approval and separate environmental review.

That distinction should be central to American Samoa's conversation.

Exploration is not mining.

Exploration is how we learn.

And remarkably, that is essentially where Eni began this conversation more than a decade and a half ago.

IMAGINE WHAT ENI WOULD ASK TODAY

None of us can say how Congressman Faleomavaega would view every aspect of today's BOEM process. We should not put words into the mouth of a leader who is no longer here to speak for himself.

But we do have his record.

And his record tells us the kinds of questions that interested him.

What minerals exist?

Where are they?

What is their strategic importance?

Does America possess the technology to responsibly recover them?

What is their economic potential?

And what role should America's Pacific territories have in understanding resources located in the vast ocean areas surrounding them?

Those were sophisticated questions in 2011.

They are even more important in 2026.

KNOWLEDGE BEFORE CONCLUSIONS

American Samoa does not need to decide today whether deep-sea mining should someday occur near our islands.

There are still enormous scientific, environmental, cultural, technological and economic questions that must be answered.

But neither should we be afraid of acquiring the information necessary to answer them. There is a profound difference between studying a resource and exploiting it. Scientific exploration gives us knowledge.

Environmental research gives us baselines.

Mapping tells us what is actually there.

And participation in the federal process gives American Samoa an opportunity to insist that our interests, culture, ocean traditions and economic aspirations are understood before decisions affecting our region are made.

We should approach this process carefully. We should demand strong environmental safeguards. We should insist upon transparency.

We should listen to fishermen, scientists, traditional leaders, environmental advocates, young people and our communities.

But we should also continue learning.

Because decisions made without knowledge are not necessarily more protective than decisions made with it.

ENI WAS LOOKING BEYOND THE HORIZON

Perhaps that is the most remarkable part of revisiting Eni Faleomavaega's words today.

In 2010 and 2011, deep-seabed critical minerals were hardly part of the everyday political conversation in American Samoa.

China's dominance of critical-mineral supply chains was not yet the major national-security issue it has become today.

And a federal critical-minerals leasing process near American Samoa probably seemed distant. Yet Eni was already looking beyond the horizon.

In fact, the phrase he used in 2010—“a more long-term vision”—may be the best description of what his record represents today.

He understood that the Pacific was not simply an empty blue space between continents.

He understood that the ocean surrounding Pacific islands held scientific, strategic and potentially economic significance that the United States had barely begun to understand.

And he believed America should find out what was there.

Now, sixteen years later, American Samoa finds itself standing at almost exactly that doorway. We do not yet know where it leads. And we certainly do not have to predetermine the destination.

But perhaps Eni's vision offers us some guidance about how to begin: Explore. Study. Document. Understand.

Then, armed with knowledge rather than speculation, make informed decisions about the future.

That was a remarkably forward-looking idea in 2011.

In 2026, it may be more relevant than ever.

(Editor’s Note: In the spirit of transparency, Samoa News notes that Michael J. McDonald is an Assistant Director of the American Samoa Port Administration. He is the Senior Advisor on deep-sea and critical minerals matters, and also serves as the chairman of the ASG Deep-Sea Minerals Steering Committee.)

Senate passes Anti‑Kickback Prohibition Act of 2026

2026-09-21

Moves to House

By

Asi Andrew Fa'asau

andrew@samoanews.com

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — The Senate has unanimously approved legislation creating the Anti‑Kickback Prohibition Act of 2026, a measure aimed at closing long‑standing gaps in procurement oversight and establishing a uniform, enforceable standard across all government entities.

According to the bill’s preamble, while certain anti‑kickback protections already exist in administrative rules and within the Procurement Act, no comprehensive, territory‑wide prohibition currently governs kickbacks, gratuities, or referral fees across all agencies and public corporations. Lawmakers say the absence of a unified standard has left room for inconsistent practices and vulnerabilities in government contracting.

The bill states that it is therefore necessary to consolidate, strengthen, and expand existing protections to ensure that government agencies, vendors, contractors, and subcontractors operate under a single, clear, and enforceable framework.

The Act establishes broad prohibitions covering every stage of government contracting. It specifies that no person may provide, offer, solicit, request, or accept any kickback, gratuity, or referral fee connected to the award of a government contract, the extension, modification, or renewal of a government contract, any procurement‑related recommendation, evaluation, or decision,  and any official action taken by a covered individual.

The bill further prohibits indirect payments made through intermediaries, affiliates, subcontractors, or related parties for the purpose of influencing government action.

KEY CONCEPT: KICKBACK VIOLATIONS

Individuals are also barred from requesting or accepting any kickback or gratuity from vendors, contractors, subcontractors, or any person seeking or performing government work.

Subcontractors are explicitly prohibited from making payments to contractors or other subcontractors to secure a subcontract award or favorable treatment under a government contract.

To strengthen transparency, the Act requires all bids, proposals, and contract submissions to disclose any commissions, fees, or compensation arrangements with third parties, any ownership, familial, or financial relationship with a covered individual, any subcontractor or intermediary receiving compensation related to the bid, and any contingent fee arrangement.

Failure to disclose required information may result in disqualification, contract termination, suspension or debarment, and civil penalties.

The bill includes provisions for reporting suspected violations and offers whistleblower protections to individuals who come forward with information.

Penalties for violations include contract termination, suspension or debarment, a $25,000 fine per violation, recovery of improperly obtained funds, voiding of contracts secured through prohibited conduct.

These measures aim to deter misconduct and ensure that government procurement processes remain fair, transparent, and accountable.

The bill, sponsored by Senator Togiola T.A. Tulafono, now moves to the House of Representatives for review.

If approved by both the House and the Governor, the Anti‑Kickback Prohibition Act of 2026 would take effect 90 days after the Governor signs it.
